extracted.intended_audience: educated British public and political leaders (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Counsel and evaluative principles for composing/assessing political polemics about revolution, constitutional change, and public rhetoric; emphasizes prudence, experience, and moral temperance over abstract theory. Drawn from an 18th-century essay arguing against radical, a priori claims and celebratory glorification of violent upheaval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for constitutional precedents and experience
rubrics_metrics.description: "the fundamental laws of their country, the fixed form of a Constitution whose merits are confirmed by the solid test of long experience and an increasing public strength and national prosperity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value established forms, precedents, charters, and acts of Parliament as tested by long experience; distrust claims that dismiss experience as 'the wisdom of unlettered men.' Do not discard institutions that have answered tolerably for ages without very strong, empirically supported reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject metaphysical absolute rights (the 'rights of men')
rubrics_metrics.description: "They have 'the rights of men.' Against these there can be no prescription; against these no argument is binding: these admit no temperament and no compromise: anything withheld from their full demand is so much of fraud and injustice."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware absolutist, metaphysical formulations of rights that disallow compromise; such claims make negotiation and governance impossible and are politically dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights within civil society derive from convention
rubrics_metrics.description: "If civil society be the offspring of convention, that convention must be its law. That convention must limit and modify all the descriptions of constitution which are formed under it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat legislative, judicial, and executive powers as creatures of social convention; do not assert rights that are 'absolutely repugnant' to the existence of civil society. Practical governance requires accepting conventions that make collective life possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man should be judge in his own cause
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the first motives to civil society, and which becomes one of its fundamental rules, is, that no man should be judge in his own cause."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impartial adjudication is a foundational political principle: entering civil society requires abandoning unilateral self-judgment and some personal claims of self-defence in favour of institutions that can adjudicate disputes fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government is a practical contrivance, not founded on abstract natural rights
rubrics_metrics.description: "Government is not made in virtue of natural rights... The science of constructing a commonwealth... is, like every other experimental science, not to be taught a priori."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach political design empirically: favour tested arrangements and cumulative experience over purely theoretical, a priori systems. Political science requires long observation and caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise extreme caution before demolishing existing institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is with infinite caution that any man ought to venture upon pulling down an edifice which has answered in any tolerable degree for ages the common purposes of society, or on building it up again without having models and patterns of approved utility before his eyes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not undertake radical reconstruction without proven models and long experience; upheaval risks unforeseen latent causes and long-term harms that short experiments cannot reveal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex, balanced constitutions over simplistic designs
rubrics_metrics.description: "The simple governments are fundamentally defective... If you were to contemplate society in but one point of view, all these simple modes of polity are infinitely captivating... But it is better that the whole, should be imperfectly and anomalously answered than that while some parts are provided for with great exactness, others might be totally neglected."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware political schemes that promise elegant simplicity; complex societies require complex institutions to address competing needs and avoid neglecting important functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand rights as compromises and balances
rubrics_metrics.description: "The rights of men are in a sort of middle, incapable of definition, but not impossible to be discerned... their advantages; and these are often in balances between differences of good,--in compromises sometimes between good and evil, and sometimes between evil and evil."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rights as practical balances among competing goods rather than absolute, precisely definable entitlements; policymaking should weigh trade-offs morally and practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between power and right; rights must be reasonable and beneficial
rubrics_metrics.description: "By these theorists the right of the people is almost always sophistically confounded with their power... Men have no right to what is not reasonable, and to what is not for their benefit."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate numerical or physical power with legitimate right. Claims of right should be judged by reasonableness and contribution to real benefit, guided by prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid habitual revolutionary rhetoric; reserve extreme remedies for extreme occasions
rubrics_metrics.description: "I never liked this continual talk of resistance and revolution, or the practice of making the extreme medicine of the Constitution its daily bread. It renders the habit of society dangerously valetudinary; it is taking periodical doses of mercury..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize the practice of treating revolution as a regular, everyday tool. Frequent invocation of extreme remedies dulls moral sensibility and weakens the capacity to respond effectively when true crises arise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of hypocritical or insincere theorists who abandon principles
rubrics_metrics.description: "Almost all the high-bred republicans of my time have, after a short space, become the most decided, thorough-paced courtiers... They see no merit in the good, and no fault in the vicious management of public affairs; they rather rejoice in the latter, as more propitious to revolution."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political actors for steadiness and practical commitment rather than rhetorical fervour; extremist theorizing often masks hypocrisy or lack of real intent to act consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not sanctify or celebrate violent atrocities in public or religious rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: "I find a preacher of the Gospel profaning the beautiful and prophetic ejaculation... and applying it, with an inhuman and unnatural rapture, to the most horrid, atrocious, and afflicting spectacle..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious and moral language should not be repurposed to glorify massacres, assassination, or other brutal acts. Public commemorations and sermons should avoid turning horror into triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative deliberation must be free from physical coercion to be legitimate
rubrics_metrics.description: "They sit in the heart... surrounded by an army not raised either by the authority of their crown nor by their command... under the terror of the bayonet, and the lamp-post, and the torch to their houses, they are obliged to adopt all the crude and desperate measures..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that assemblies deciding under threat, mob pressure, or military force lack genuine liberty and impartiality; legitimacy requires deliberative independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard public deliberation against mob-driven clubs and seminaries of sedition
rubrics_metrics.description: "Their measures are decided before they are debated... suggested by clubs composed of a monstrous medley of all conditions, tongues, and nations... in academies, intended as so many seminaries for these clubs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of policies formed in popular clubs, mobs, or fevered societies where violent or daring counsel is prized as 'genius.' Promote sober, considered debate free from mob influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain humanity and compassion in political conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: "Humanity and compassion are ridiculed as the fruits of superstition and ignorance. Tenderness to individuals is considered as treason to the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve compassion and tenderness even when political passions run high; dehumanizing opponents or victims undermines moral legitimacy and social cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality pertains to rights, not to equal material outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: "In this partnership all men have equal rights; but not to equal things. He that has but five shillings in the partnership has as good a right to it as he that has five hundred pounds has to his larger proportion; but he has not a right to an equal dividend..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing about equality, distinguish equal legal/political rights from equal shares of wealth or outcomes; rights ensure fair participation, not forced material parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize restraints as part of rights; rights vary with circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: "In this sense the restraints on men, as well as their liberties, are to be reckoned among their rights. But as the liberties and the restrictions vary with times and circumstances, and admit of infinite modifications, they cannot be settled upon any abstract rule..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reasonable restraints within the conception of rights; avoid abstract, one-size-fits-all rules when allocating liberties and limits—context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply political reason as a moral arithmetic, not metaphysical certainties
rubrics_metrics.description: "Political reason is a computing principle: adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing, morally, and not metaphysically or mathematically, true moral denominations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prudential, comparative judgment—weigh costs and benefits morally—rather than appeal to abstract metaphysical formulas when making political decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider historical judgment and long-term consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: "History, who keeps a durable record of all our acts, and exercises her awful censure over the proceedings of all sorts of sovereigns, will not forget either those events... History will record, that, on the morning of the sixth of October, 1789..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When forming public rhetoric or taking political actions, anticipate how historians and posterity will judge them; short-term triumphs can become long-term moral stains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cruelty and scorn when granting amnesty or consolation
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is a topic of consolation which our ordinary of Newgate would be too humane to use to a criminal at the foot of the gallows... Thus to administer the opiate potion of amnesty, powdered with all the ingredients of scorn and contempt, is to hold to his lips... the cup of human misery."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not cloak amnesty or reconciliation in insults or scorn; compassionate, respectful treatment of victims and those punished preserves moral dignity and avoids compounding injury.
